# Aim

Predict, and describe the predictors of, high **COSMIC** somatic-data utility
across dominant DDG2P genes. One random-forest model on a
lean feature set, evaluated by **fold-aware repeated cross-validation** (the
network-proximity feature is recomputed inside each fold, seeded on that fold's
training genes only — leakage-safe). A penalised/plain logistic regression gives
interpretable odds ratios. Grey-zone genes are scored but not trained on.

Inputs: `gene_heterogeneity_feature_matrix.csv` (from
`Build_gene_feature_matrix.Rmd`) and the STRING graph (`network_features.R`).

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(randomForest)
library(pROC)
library(PRROC)
library(glmnet)
library(fastshap)   # Monte-Carlo-approximate Shapley values, model-agnostic
library(shapviz)    # SHAP summary/beeswarm plotting
source("network_features.R")   # load_string_graph(), network_contrast()
set.seed(42)
theme_set(theme_bw(12))

# ---- config ----
# All the "knobs" for this analysis are collected here at the top, so the
# rest of the script can refer to them by name instead of scattering magic
# numbers through the code below.
RESTART   <- 0.5     # RWR restart probability (network_contrast(); POC default)
STRING_THR<- 700     # STRING combined_score cutoff for a "high-confidence" PPI edge
N_FOLDS   <- 5        # number of cross-validation folds per repeat
N_REPEATS <- 10       # number of times the whole 5-fold CV is repeated (with fresh fold assignments), for a more stable performance estimate
N_TREES   <- 2000     # number of trees in every random forest fit (CV folds and the final full-data model)
BOOT_IMP  <- 200     # bootstrap replicates for ridge-OR CI stability
N_SHAP_SIM<- 100      # Monte-Carlo repetitions per gene for fastshap::explain()

# The 9 gene-level features the model is actually fitted on. Every name here
# must be a column in the feature matrix loaded below (see `feat`).
FEATURES  <- c("dd_altfunc", "dd_lof", "cancer_oncogene_missense", "cancer_tsg",
               "loeuf", "moeuf", "exp_mis", "hotspot_count", "net_contrast")
# constraint_missing / network_missing were tested as features and dropped:
# both had negligible SHAP magnitude and a ridge OR CI
# spanning ~1, i.e. uninformative. They are still COMPUTED and reported in the
# exported prediction table (diagnostic: which genes had an imputed value),
# just no longer fed into either model.
CONT_FEATS<- c("loeuf", "moeuf", "exp_mis")   # constraint metrics that may be NA

OUT_FIG   <- "../../../Data/Figures/Final/Supplement/Gene_heterogeneity_model.png"
OUT_PRED  <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_predictions.csv"
OUT_SHAP  <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_shap_summary.csv"
OUT_OR    <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_ridge_or.csv"
```

```{r load}
# Load the per-gene feature matrix built by Build_gene_feature_matrix.Rmd. Every
# row is one gene, with the label (positive/negative/grey) and the non-network
# features already attached; the network-proximity feature is NOT in this file
# because it has to be computed fold-aware (see Section 2 below), so it's added
# later, separately, inside the CV loop and the full-model chunk.
feat <- read_csv("../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_feature_matrix.csv",
                 show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  # dd_altfunc / dd_lof / cancer_oncogene_missense / cancer_tsg are already 0/1
  # integers (independent binary flags -- a gene can be any combination); kept
  # numeric (not factor) so glm() reports a directly interpretable per-flag
  # odds ratio, and randomForest splits on them same as any binary variable.
  mutate(constraint_missing = as.integer(is.na(loeuf)))   # flag before imputation

# Split into the genes we actually have a training label for (lab: positive or
# negative only -- "grey" genes are deliberately excluded from training because
# their AUC confidence interval didn't clearly support either class) and the
# grey-zone genes themselves (grey), which the fitted model will later be asked
# to score/predict on, not train on.
lab <- feat %>% filter(label %in% c("positive", "negative")) %>%
  mutate(y = factor(if_else(label == "positive", "pos", "neg"),
                    levels = c("neg", "pos")))
grey <- feat %>% filter(label == "grey")
cat(sprintf("labelled: %d (pos=%d, neg=%d) | grey: %d\n",
            nrow(lab), sum(lab$y == "pos"), sum(lab$y == "neg"), nrow(grey)))

# Build the STRING protein-protein interaction graph once here (it's the same
# graph for every fold and for the final full-data fit) -- only the SEEDS used
# to walk it change between folds.
graph <- load_string_graph(STRING_THR)
cat("STRING graph:", vcount(graph), "genes,", ecount(graph), "edges\n")
cat("labelled genes absent from STRING:",
    sum(!lab$gene %in% V(graph)$name), "\n")
```

# 1. Missing-value handling (median-impute + flags)

Constraint metrics (`loeuf`/`moeuf`/`exp_mis`) and the network feature are
median-imputed, with explicit missingness flags (`constraint_missing`,
`network_missing`) computed alongside. These flags were tested as model
features and dropped (see `FEATURES` above): both had
negligible SHAP magnitude and a ridge odds-ratio CI spanning 1, i.e.
uninformative. They are still reported as diagnostic columns in the exported
prediction table (which genes had an imputed value), just not used as
predictors. `constraint_missing` is set above from the original
(pre-imputation) matrix; `network_missing` is set once on the full data in the
full-model chunk (Section 3) for reporting -- the CV loop (Section 2) no
longer needs to track it per-fold, since it is not a model feature. Imputation
medians are always learned from **training** genes within CV so the estimate
stays honest; imputation is done inline in the CV and full-model chunks below.

# 2. Fold-aware repeated cross-validation

```{r cv, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Assigns each gene to one of k folds SEPARATELY within each class (pos/neg),
# so every fold ends up with roughly the same pos:neg ratio as the full
# labelled set ("stratified" folds). Without stratifying, a fold could by
# chance end up almost all-negative, making AUC unstable/meaningless for that
# fold given how few positives there are in total.
strat_folds <- function(y, k) {
  # stratified fold ids
  fid <- integer(length(y))
  for (lev in levels(y)) {
    idx <- which(y == lev)
    fid[idx] <- sample(rep_len(1:k, length(idx)))
  }
  fid
}

# Repeated k-fold CV: run the whole 5-fold split N_REPEATS times, each time
# with a fresh random fold assignment. A single 5-fold split is noisy with
# this few labelled genes (which genes happen to land in which fold matters);
# averaging performance over many different splits gives a much more stable
# estimate of how well the model actually generalises.
cv_scores <- tibble()
for (rep_i in seq_len(N_REPEATS)) {
  folds <- strat_folds(lab$y, N_FOLDS)
  for (f in seq_len(N_FOLDS)) {
    # Split into this fold's training genes (tr, folds != f) and held-out test
    # genes (te, folds == f). Everything computed below -- the network seeds,
    # the imputation medians, the fitted forest -- is derived from `tr` only,
    # and then simply APPLIED to `te`. This is what makes the fold "honest":
    # no information from the held-out genes leaks into how they get scored.
    tr <- lab[folds != f, ]; te <- lab[folds == f, ]
    pos_seeds <- tr$gene[tr$y == "pos"]; neg_seeds <- tr$gene[tr$y == "neg"]

    # fold-aware network contrast: seeds = TRAINING genes only.
    # Held-out test genes are scored against the FULL training-seed set --
    # this is already leakage-safe on its own, since a held-out gene is never
    # a member of tr and so can never be a seed for its own score.
    nc_test <- network_contrast(graph, pos_seeds, neg_seeds,
                                query = te$gene, restart = RESTART)

    # Training genes, in contrast, DO sit inside pos_seeds/neg_seeds by
    # construction -- so scoring them against the same seed sets used above
    # would self-seed every training gene (leaving each one's own vote in its
    # own class's network walk). This is the same self-seeding inflation
    # documented and fixed for the full-data model in Section 3 (~3.6x
    # apparent class-separation inflation, some genes sign-flipped) -- left
    # uncorrected here it would still bias what the forest learns about
    # net_contrast during training, even though it doesn't directly leak any
    # test-gene label. Fixed the same way as Section 3: leave-one-out, i.e.
    # each training gene's own value is computed with that gene excluded from
    # its own class's seed set (all OTHER training genes are still seeds as
    # normal). This is more expensive (one network_contrast call per training
    # gene rather than one for the whole fold) but cheap enough in practice
    # (STRING graph RWR takes ~30ms per call) to do exactly, rather than
    # approximate.
    nc_train <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, nrow(tr)), tr$gene)
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(tr))) {
      g_i <- tr$gene[i]
      pos_i <- setdiff(pos_seeds, g_i); neg_i <- setdiff(neg_seeds, g_i)
      nc_train[g_i] <- network_contrast(graph, pos_i, neg_i, query = g_i, restart = RESTART)[g_i]
    }

    net_med <- median(nc_train, na.rm = TRUE)     # impute from training only (now leave-one-out corrected)
    tr$net_contrast <- ifelse(is.na(nc_train[tr$gene]), net_med, nc_train[tr$gene])
    te$net_contrast <- ifelse(is.na(nc_test[te$gene]), net_med, nc_test[te$gene])

    # constraint imputation from training medians
    # Same honesty principle applied to the constraint features (loeuf/moeuf/
    # exp_mis): the imputation value (the median) is calculated from training
    # genes only, then used to fill gaps in BOTH tr and te. Computing the
    # median from the combined tr+te set would let information about which
    # genes are in the test fold subtly influence the imputed values.
    for (v in CONT_FEATS) {
      m <- median(tr[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
      tr[[v]] <- ifelse(is.na(tr[[v]]), m, tr[[v]])
      te[[v]] <- ifelse(is.na(te[[v]]), m, te[[v]])
    }

    # Fit a random forest on this fold's training genes only. `strata`/
    # `sampsize` tell randomForest to build each tree from a balanced
    # bootstrap sample (n_min positives AND n_min negatives, where n_min is
    # the size of the smaller class) rather than the natural, imbalanced
    # class ratio -- otherwise, with far more negatives than positives, the
    # forest would be biased toward always predicting "negative".
    n_min <- min(table(tr$y))
    rf <- randomForest(x = tr[, FEATURES], y = tr$y, ntree = N_TREES,
                       strata = tr$y, sampsize = c(neg = n_min, pos = n_min))
    # Predict the probability of being "positive" for the held-out genes, and
    # stash it alongside their true label so performance can be assessed
    # afterwards across every fold/repeat at once.
    p <- predict(rf, te[, FEATURES], type = "prob")[, "pos"]
    cv_scores <- bind_rows(cv_scores,
      tibble(rep = rep_i, fold = f, gene = te$gene, truth = te$y, prob = p))
  }
}

# CV performance: pool held-out predictions, compute per-repeat AUC/AUPRC then average
# For each repeat, gather every gene's held-out prediction (across its 5
# folds) and compute one AUC (ranking ability) and one AUPRC (precision-recall
# area, more informative than AUC when positives are rare) for that repeat.
# Averaging across the N_REPEATS independent repeats (rather than reporting a
# single repeat's number) gives both a point estimate and a sense of how
# variable that estimate is (SD) due to the specific random fold assignment.
perf <- cv_scores %>% group_by(rep) %>% summarise(
  auc = as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(truth, prob, levels = c("neg","pos"),
                                       direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))),
  auprc = {
    pr <- PRROC::pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob[truth=="pos"],
                          scores.class1 = prob[truth=="neg"])
    pr$auc.integral
  }, .groups = "drop")
cat(sprintf("Cross-validated AUC:  %.3f (SD %.3f)\n", mean(perf$auc), sd(perf$auc)))
cat(sprintf("Cross-validated AUPRC: %.3f (SD %.3f)\n", mean(perf$auprc), sd(perf$auprc)))
```

# 3. Full-data model: importance, odds ratios, grey-zone scoring

```{r full-model, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Section 2 (above) answered "how well would this model generalise" via CV.
# This section instead fits ONE model on ALL labelled genes at once (the best
# use of the data we have), to (a) report which features matter and in which
# direction (SHAP + ridge odds ratios) and (b) actually score the grey-zone
# genes that were held out of labelling entirely. None of this chunk's numbers
# should be read as a performance estimate -- for that, see the CV results
# above.
#
# Re-seed explicitly here, rather than relying on the single global seed set
# in `setup`. randomForest()'s internal random draws (bagging, mtry selection)
# depend on the actual VALUES of the input features, not just their
# dimensions -- confirmed empirically -- so without this, any unrelated change
# upstream (e.g. to the CV loop in Section 2, which touches none of this
# chunk's own inputs) would silently shift the RNG stream inherited here and
# change the reported SHAP values, ridge odds ratios, and grey-zone
# predictions by chance alone, even though nothing about this model itself
# had changed. Re-seeding makes this chunk's results reproducible on their own
# terms, independent of anything computed above it.
set.seed(42)
all_pos <- lab$gene[lab$y == "pos"]; all_neg <- lab$gene[lab$y == "neg"]

# Grey-zone / candidate-gene scoring: seed on ALL labelled genes. This is
# correct and unbiased here -- grey genes are never seeds, so this matches the
# real-world use case ("given everything labelled so far, where does this new
# gene sit?").
nc_all <- network_contrast(graph, all_pos, all_neg,
                          query = feat$gene, restart = RESTART)

# Labelled genes: seeding each gene's own class network WITH that gene itself
# (as nc_all does) leaks the gene's own label into its own feature value. This
# is NOT a small effect: checked empirically by comparing to a proper
# leave-one-out (LOO) computation -- mean class separation (pos - neg) in
# log10 RWR-ratio units is ~4.6 with self-seeding vs ~1.3 with honest LOO (a
# ~3.6x inflation), and individual genes can flip sign once their own vote is
# removed. For labelled genes, net_contrast is therefore recomputed leaving
# each gene out of its own class's seed set, mirroring the fold-aware
# safeguard already used for CV in Section 2. (The CV performance metric above
# is unaffected by this leak: held-out test genes are never in their own
# fold's seed set to begin with.)
nc_loo <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, nrow(lab)), lab$gene)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(lab))) {
  g <- lab$gene[i]
  pos_i <- setdiff(all_pos, g); neg_i <- setdiff(all_neg, g)
  nc_loo[g] <- network_contrast(graph, pos_i, neg_i, query = g, restart = RESTART)[g]
}
nc_for_feat <- nc_all
nc_for_feat[names(nc_loo)] <- nc_loo   # overwrite labelled genes with the honest LOO value
net_med <- median(nc_loo, na.rm = TRUE)   # honest (LOO) imputation median


# Build the full (every gene: positive/negative/grey) feature table, using the
# honest (LOO-corrected for labelled genes, self-seeded-but-unbiased for grey
# genes) network feature computed above, and flag which genes had no network
# score at all (absent from STRING) so that's visible downstream.
full <- feat %>%
  mutate(net_contrast = ifelse(is.na(nc_for_feat[gene]), net_med, nc_for_feat[gene]),
         network_missing = as.integer(is.na(nc_for_feat[gene])))
# Constraint-feature imputation here uses the median across all LABELLED genes
# only (label != "grey"), matching the CV loop's principle of never letting
# the genes being scored/predicted influence the value they get imputed to.
for (v in CONT_FEATS) {
  m <- median(full[[v]][full$label != "grey"], na.rm = TRUE)
  full[[v]] <- ifelse(is.na(full[[v]]), m, full[[v]])
}
lab_full <- full %>% filter(label %in% c("positive","negative")) %>%
  mutate(y = factor(if_else(label=="positive","pos","neg"), levels=c("neg","pos")))

# RF on all labelled genes
# Same class-balanced bootstrap-sampling approach as each CV fold (see
# Section 2), but now trained on every labelled gene at once -- this is the
# single model whose feature importances/SHAP values and grey-zone
# predictions are reported below. `importance = TRUE` retains randomForest's
# own permutation-importance scores as a cross-check against the SHAP ranking.
n_min <- min(table(lab_full$y))
rf_full <- randomForest(x = lab_full[, FEATURES], y = lab_full$y, ntree = N_TREES,
                       importance = TRUE, strata = lab_full$y,
                       sampsize = c(neg = n_min, pos = n_min))

# SHAP (Shapley value) summary: shows magnitude AND direction per feature,
# unlike bare permutation importance (magnitude only). fastshap computes
# model-agnostic Monte-Carlo-approximate Shapley values (N_SHAP_SIM repetitions
# per gene) via a predict-probability wrapper; shapviz turns the resulting
# gene x feature SHAP matrix into a beeswarm plot (features ordered by mean
# |SHAP|, points coloured by that gene's feature value, position = SHAP value
# i.e. that feature's push toward/away from "high somatic utility" for that
# gene). baseline = the RF's average predicted probability of "pos" (the
# reference point SHAP values are measured against).
shap_pfun <- function(object, newdata) predict(object, newdata = newdata, type = "prob")[, "pos"]
X_shap <- as.data.frame(lab_full[, FEATURES])
shap_vals <- fastshap::explain(rf_full, X = X_shap, pred_wrapper = shap_pfun, nsim = N_SHAP_SIM)
shap_baseline <- mean(shap_pfun(rf_full, X_shap))
sv_rf <- shapviz(as.matrix(shap_vals), X = X_shap, baseline = shap_baseline)

# Interpretable multivariable model -> odds ratios via RIDGE-penalised logistic
# regression (glmnet, alpha = 0), NOT plain glm(). With 40 events across 9
# features -- some structurally correlated, e.g. cancer_oncogene_missense with
# dd_altfunc, since the manuscript's AltFunc group is defined as their
# intersection -- plain glm() showed COMPLETE SEPARATION when tested (residual
# deviance ~0, every fitted probability at the 0/1 boundary, coefficient SEs of
# order 1e5): confirmed empirically, not just a theoretical risk. Ridge
# regularisation shrinks all coefficients to finite, stable values while
# keeping every feature in the model (appropriate here since the goal is one
# interpretable estimate per feature, not sparse selection). glmnet has no
# analytic CIs, so we bootstrap coefficients at a FIXED lambda (selected once
# via lambda.1se on the full labelled set) to get percentile 95% intervals --
# the same resample-and-refit logic already used for the RF importance
# bootstrap above.
#
# Continuous/count features (loeuf, moeuf, exp_mis, hotspot_count,
# net_contrast) are z-scored before fitting, so every OR below is per 1-SD
# increase; binary features (0/1) are left as-is, so their OR is already a
# natural per-unit (absent->present) contrast. Without this, a raw-unit OR for
# a feature ranging 0-48 (hotspot_count) or 200-7000 (exp_mis) looks
# artificially close to 1 next to a 0/1 feature, even when both carry
# comparable information -- this is a real, checked distortion, not
# just a hypothetical concern.
STD_FEATS <- c("loeuf", "moeuf", "exp_mis", "hotspot_count", "net_contrast")
lab_full_std <- lab_full
for (v in STD_FEATS) lab_full_std[[v]] <- as.numeric(scale(lab_full_std[[v]]))
x_mat <- as.matrix(lab_full_std[, FEATURES])
y01   <- as.integer(lab_full$y == "pos")
stopifnot(!anyNA(x_mat))

# Lambda is selected by LEAVE-ONE-OUT cross-validation (nfolds = number of
# labelled genes), not the random N_FOLDS-fold CV used for model performance
# in Section 2, because random 5-fold CV picks a genuinely different
# lambda.1se (and hence a materially different ridge OR point estimate -- up
# to ~30% swings for the most correlated features, e.g.
# cancer_oncogene_missense) depending on which random fold split happens to
# be drawn, even with a fixed seed elsewhere in the script (the fold split
# itself is a further random draw). With only 124 labelled genes, a 5-fold
# split is small enough for this fold-assignment noise to move the CV error
# curve enough to select a different penalty. Leave-one-out CV has a unique,
# deterministic fold assignment (each gene held out exactly once), which
# removes this instability entirely: it gives an identical lambda_sel and OR
# point estimates across repeated runs with different seeds. The percentile
# bootstrap CI below (at this fixed lambda) is unaffected and is already stable
# at BOOT_IMP=200.
cv_ridge   <- cv.glmnet(x_mat, y01, family = "binomial", alpha = 0, nfolds = nrow(x_mat))
lambda_sel <- cv_ridge$lambda.1se
cat(sprintf("Ridge penalty selected (lambda.1se): %.4f\n", lambda_sel))

fit_ridge <- glmnet(x_mat, y01, family = "binomial", alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_sel)
point_tab <- as.matrix(coef(fit_ridge)) %>%
  {tibble(term = rownames(.), beta = .[, 1])} %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)")

or_boot <- map_dfr(seq_len(BOOT_IMP), function(b) {
  bi <- sample(nrow(lab_full), replace = TRUE)
  xb <- x_mat[bi, , drop = FALSE]; yb <- y01[bi]
  if (length(unique(yb)) < 2) return(NULL)
  fit_b <- glmnet(xb, yb, family = "binomial", alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_sel)
  cf <- as.matrix(coef(fit_b))
  tibble(term = rownames(cf), beta = cf[, 1], b = b) %>% filter(term != "(Intercept)")
})

or_tab <- or_boot %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  summarise(conf.low = quantile(beta, .025), conf.high = quantile(beta, .975), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(point_tab, by = "term") %>%
  transmute(term, estimate = exp(beta), conf.low = exp(conf.low), conf.high = exp(conf.high))

# Score grey-zone (and all) genes
full$pred_prob <- predict(rf_full, full[, FEATURES], type = "prob")[, "pos"]

# Numeric SHAP summary: mean |SHAP| per feature (for citing exact magnitudes of
# importance in the manuscript text) and a direction indicator = the Spearman
# correlation, across labelled genes, between each feature's own value and its
# own SHAP value (positive = higher feature values push toward "high somatic
# utility"). NB: the naive alternative, mean SIGNED SHAP, is NOT used here --
# checked directly and found to be ~1000x smaller than mean |SHAP| and to
# flip sign across independent Monte-Carlo reruns (SHAP values are ~zero-mean
# by construction, since they sum to explain deviations from a fixed baseline
# across the same data used to set that baseline), so it is pure noise, not a
# usable direction summary. Read direction from this correlation, or from the
# beeswarm colouring in the figure, not from an average signed SHAP value.
shap_mat  <- as.matrix(shap_vals)
shap_summ <- tibble(
    feature = colnames(shap_mat),
    mean_abs = colMeans(abs(shap_mat)),
    direction_corr = vapply(colnames(shap_mat), function(f)
      suppressWarnings(cor(X_shap[[f]], shap_mat[, f], method = "spearman")),
      numeric(1))
  ) %>% arrange(desc(mean_abs))
cat("\nSHAP summary (ranked by mean |SHAP|; direction_corr = Spearman corr of feature value vs its SHAP value):\n")
print(shap_summ, n = Inf)

# Exported for the feature-dictionary supplementary table (Supplementary Table
# 8), which merges these with a hand-written description/source per feature.
write_csv(shap_summ, OUT_SHAP)
write_csv(or_tab, OUT_OR)
```

# 4. Figure + prediction table

```{r figure, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=13, fig.height=5}
# Panel (a): SHAP beeswarm. Each dot is one labelled gene's SHAP value for one
# feature (features stacked top-to-bottom, most important -- highest mean
# |SHAP| -- at the top); dot colour = that gene's raw value for the feature
# (shapviz's default palette); dot x-position = how much that feature pushed
# THIS gene's prediction up (toward "high somatic utility") or down, relative
# to the baseline. The CV AUC/AUPRC (Section 2) is printed in the subtitle so
# the reader always sees the honest performance figure alongside the
# full-data importance plot, not just the (necessarily rosier) in-sample fit.
p_imp <- sv_importance(sv_rf, kind = "bee") +
  labs(title = "(a) Random-forest SHAP summary",
       subtitle = sprintf("CV AUC %.2f, AUPRC %.2f", mean(perf$auc), mean(perf$auprc)))

# Panel (b): ridge odds ratios as a forest plot. Terms are ordered by their
# point estimate (fct_reorder) so the plot reads top-to-bottom from strongest
# positive to strongest negative association; the dashed vertical line at
# OR = 1 marks "no association"; x is on a log scale, which is the natural
# scale for odds ratios (an OR of 2 and an OR of 0.5 are equally far from 1).
p_or <- or_tab %>%
  mutate(term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "(b) Ridge logistic regression",
       subtitle = "Ridge-penalised (bootstrap 95% CI)",
       x = "Odds ratio for high somatic utility (log scale)", y = NULL)

# Combine both panels side by side with patchwork, and add a shared caption
# (rather than repeating it per-panel) reminding the reader how to interpret
# the OR scale in panel (b).
fig <- patchwork::wrap_plots(p_imp, p_or, ncol = 2) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(caption = paste(
    "Ridge odds ratios (b): continuous features standardised per 1-SD;",
    "binary features per unit (absent -> present)."))
ggsave(OUT_FIG, fig, width = 13, height = 5.3, dpi = 300)
fig

# Export the full per-gene table (every gene: positive/negative/grey) with its
# features, its original benchmarking AUC, and this model's predicted
# probability of "high somatic utility" (pred_prob) -- this becomes the
# feature-dictionary / per-gene-prediction supplementary table. Sorted with
# the most-confidently-predicted-useful genes first.
full %>%
  select(gene, label, auc, auc_lower, auc_upper, all_of(FEATURES),
         constraint_missing, network_missing, pred_prob) %>%
  arrange(desc(pred_prob)) %>%
  write_csv(OUT_PRED)
cat("Wrote:", OUT_FIG, "and", OUT_PRED, "\n")

# sanity checks
# The RASopathy genes are the paper's own worked example of genes with
# excellent somatic-data utility, so as a quick plausibility check, print
# their predicted probabilities here and eyeball that they come out high.
cat("\nRASopathy genes (expect high pred_prob):\n")
full %>% filter(gene %in% c("PTPN11","KRAS","HRAS","BRAF","MAP2K1","RIT1")) %>%
  select(gene, label, pred_prob) %>% print()
```

> Caveats to carry into the manuscript: (i) small positive class (40) — CV, not
> training, performance is reported; (ii) hotspot count, exp_mis and the
> network feature partly derive from somatic / mutation-model / label-seeded
> data (flagged in Discussion); the network feature is fold-aware for CV, and
> for the full-model figure/table labelled genes' net_contrast is computed
> leave-one-out (each gene excluded from its own class's seed set) to avoid the
> substantial self-seeding inflation this produces
> (~3.6x apparent class-separation inflation, some genes sign-flipped) — only
> grey-zone genes use the seed-on-all-labelled version, which is unbiased since
> they are never seeds; (iii) mechanism defines the original gene groups, so it
> is expected to be a leading
> predictor; (iv) the multivariable odds ratios use RIDGE-penalised (not plain)
> logistic regression, with bootstrap (not analytic) confidence intervals --
> plain glm() was tested first and showed complete separation on this dataset
> (residual deviance ~0, all fitted probabilities at the 0/1 boundary), so the
> reported odds ratios are regularised/shrunk towards 1 and should be described
> as such, not as unpenalised maximum-likelihood estimates; (v) the RF panel
> shows Shapley (SHAP) values, giving both magnitude and direction per feature
> (unlike bare permutation importance, which is magnitude-only) -- these are
> Monte-Carlo-approximate (fastshap, N_SHAP_SIM repetitions per gene), not exact
> TreeSHAP, so expect small run-to-run numerical noise at fixed N_SHAP_SIM;
> (vi) the model's strongest predictors (hotspot_count, net_contrast, the
> cancer CGC flags) are themselves somatic/cancer-domain annotations, so most
> of its discriminative power reflects overlap between the label and other
> somatic-data sources rather than gene properties independent of somatic
> data -- this should be stated explicitly in the Discussion rather than
> implied.
